result:
The design's key choice is that the tenant comes from the credential and never from the URL, so a client cannot address another tenant's data at all.

```
GET|POST          /v1/collections
GET|PATCH|DELETE  /v1/collections/{col_id}
GET|POST          /v1/collections/{col_id}/documents
GET|PUT|PATCH|DELETE /v1/documents/{doc_id}
GET               /v1/documents/{doc_id}/revisions
GET               /v1/documents/{doc_id}/revisions/{rev}
POST              /v1/documents/{doc_id}/restore      {"revision": 7}
GET|POST|DELETE   /v1/api-keys[/{key_id}]
```

**Resources.** IDs are opaque, prefixed and globally unique (`doc_01J...`, UUIDv7 underneath), which is why documents can be addressed flat while being listed under their collection. A document is an envelope (`id`, `collection_id`, `revision`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, `data`), so system fields never collide with user fields. `PUT` replaces, `PATCH` is JSON Merge Patch, and `DELETE` is a soft delete, so restore works.

**Concurrency.** Every write to an existing document requires `If-Match` with the ETag (the revision number). A stale ETag returns 412 and a missing one returns 428, so lost updates are impossible rather than merely unlikely. `POST` accepts an `Idempotency-Key`, so retries do not create duplicates.

**Auth.** Requests carry `Authorization: Bearer`, with either a short-lived OAuth2 JWT for users or a tenant-bound API key for services. Both resolve to exactly one `tenant_id` plus scopes (`documents:read`, `documents:write`, `collections:admin`), and a user in two tenants gets two tokens. Enforce the tenant in the data layer as well (row-level security or a mandatory tenant key prefix), so that a forgotten handler check fails closed. An ID in another tenant returns 404, not 403, so existence does not leak; 403 means your own tenant but an insufficient scope.

**Pagination.** Lists use `?limit=50&cursor=...` (max 200) and return `{"data": [...], "next_cursor": "..." | null}`. The cursor is opaque and encodes a keyset position on `(created_at, id)` plus the active filter and sort. This stays stable under concurrent writes and costs the same at any depth, which offset pagination does not. There is no total count, because it is expensive at scale and clients rarely need it.

**Versioning.** The major version lives in the path because it is visible in logs, trivial to route and easy to use from curl. Additive changes (new fields, new endpoints) ship in place, so clients must ignore unknown fields. Breaking changes go to `/v2`, with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers on `/v1`. Document history is the separate `revisions` sub-resource; revisions are immutable, and restore writes a new revision rather than rewinding.

**Errors.** All errors use RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`, extended with a stable machine code and a request ID:

```json
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/validation",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 422,
  "code": "validation_failed",
  "detail": "2 fields are invalid.",
  "request_id": "req_01J8...",
  "errors": [{"field": "data.title", "code": "required"}]
}
```

Clients branch on `code` and never on `detail`, which leaves the wording free to change. The remaining statuses are 400 for malformed requests, 401, 409 for an idempotency key reused with a different body, and 429 with `Retry-After`, rate limited per tenant.

I left out search, bulk operations, webhooks and per-document ACLs; the last is the one to decide early, because it changes the authorisation model rather than just adding endpoints.
